name: Xylitol gum

card.summary: Xylitol-sweetened gum that trials link to lower plaque bacteria; benefits beyond plaque are less settled.
card.note: Highly toxic to dogs; high intake can be laxative.

quick.overview:
Xylitol gum is chewing gum sweetened with a sugar alcohol instead of sugar. Users chew it to cut down plaque bacteria and get more saliva.

Several randomized trials measured mutans streptococci and plaque, and a 2022 review cited by Wikipedia found reduced plaque. Cochrane found the evidence for most xylitol products insufficient.
quick.mechanism: Xylitol is thought to suppress growth of pathogenic oral streptococci, and chewing stimulates saliva.
quick.risks: High intake can cause gas and diarrhea. Xylitol is toxic to dogs, and the FDA considers it safe as a sweetener for people.

lead: Xylitol gum is chewing gum sweetened with xylitol, a sugar alcohol, rather than sugar. People use it to support the look of a healthy smile: it is chewed to stimulate saliva, freshen breath and reduce plaque and the cavity-causing bacteria that can lead to visible decay and stained, damaged teeth.[1][2][8]

Trials have measured mutans streptococci in plaque and saliva after xylitol gum, including a dose-response study of 132 participants.[1] A 2022 review cited by Wikipedia found that xylitol chewing gum reduces plaque, while a 2015 Cochrane review found insufficient evidence for most xylitol products other than fluoride toothpaste.[2]

Systematic reviews published between 2020 and 2025 have pooled trials of xylitol and other sugar-free gums on plaque, mutans streptococci and caries, and found that xylitol gum often performed better than sorbitol gum in head-to-head comparisons, though the trials differ in design.[9][10][11]

chain: Chewing stimulates saliva and xylitol is not fermented to acid
Plaque and mutans streptococci levels fall in trials
Cleaner, healthier-looking teeth and fresher breath
angle.text: Xylitol gum is chewed between meals as an add-on to brushing, mainly to keep teeth free of plaque and decay and to freshen breath. The appearance benefit is through tooth condition and breath rather than a direct cosmetic change.

Laxative effect at high intake; toxic to dogs

paras: Xylitol is a sugar alcohol (C5H12O5) with sweetness roughly equal to sucrose and about 40 percent fewer calories, at 2.4 kcal per gram.[2] It is manufactured industrially by hydrogenating xylose, and is used in gum, mints, candy and some toothpastes.[2] In the US the FDA approves it as a food additive and considers it safe for humans; in the EU it carries the code E967 and tabletop sweeteners must carry a laxative warning.[2]

Chewing gum itself is an old dental-hygiene idea: Wikipedia notes that dentist William F. Semple patented a gum intended to clean teeth in 1869.[8] Gum sweetened with xylitol replaces the sugar that would otherwise feed mouth bacteria.

Emil Fischer and Rudolf Stahel isolated xylitol from beech wood chips in September 1890 and named it Xylit, and Bertrand isolated xylitol syrup from straw in 1891.[2] Sugar rationing during the Second World War increased interest in sugar substitutes including xylitol.[2] Dental trials of xylitol gum followed from the 1980s, including a 1984 study of plaque and salivary S. mutans levels and a 24-month school-based caries study published in 1990.[5][4]

Xylitol specifically inhibits Streptococcus mutans, a bacterium that contributes to tooth decay, and it is not fermented to acid, according to Wikipedia's chewing gum article. The same article notes that gum stimulates saliva, which can help buffer acid and promote enamel remineralization, and that some studies attribute part of the caries benefit to chewing itself rather than only to the sweetener.[8] Wikipedia's xylitol article likewise describes the suppression of pathogenic oral streptococci.[2]

Gum is also regarded as a way to freshen breath, mostly by increasing saliva flow and helping clear food particles and bacteria, and the American Dental Association is cited as advising sugar-free gum for about 20 minutes after meals.[8]

In a randomized dose-response trial, participants chewed gum providing 0 (control), 3.44, 6.88 or 10.32 g of xylitol daily and had mutans streptococci measured at baseline, 5 weeks and 6 months.[1] Wikipedia's chewing gum article reports that this 2006 study found daily xylitol doses below about 3.4 g ineffective and no added benefit above about 10.3 g.[8][1] Another trial in young adults compared xylitol gum, probiotic gum, a combination and placebo gum over several weeks.[3]

A 2025 systematic review compared xylitol gum with polyol control gums. Searching about 900 titles for each outcome, it reviewed 16 articles on mutans streptococci, ten on plaque and five on caries. In 12 of 14 studies xylitol gum lowered mutans streptococci counts compared with sorbitol gum, plaque fell in 6 of 10 studies, and caries occurrence was lower in 3 of 5 trials. Trials with maltitol gum controls gave conflicting results.[9]

A 2022 review of xylitol gum and candies (14 articles, 16 studies from 1971 to 2020) found that in 13 of 14 gum studies plaque accumulation decreased, with six showing a reduction versus sorbitol gum and three versus gum base or no gum. Fair-quality candy studies showed no change in plaque.[10]

A 2020 meta-analysis of 12 trials of sugar-free gum reported a caries preventive fraction of 28 percent, and 33 percent among eight xylitol-only gum trials, with high heterogeneity and moderate trial quality, which the authors described as tentative evidence.[11] A 2022 meta-analysis of eight studies reported that sugar-free gum significantly reduced plaque quantity.[12] A 2015 Cochrane review cited by Wikipedia found xylitol-containing fluoride toothpaste reduced decay more than fluoride-only toothpaste, while considering evidence for other xylitol products insufficient.[2]

High intakes of xylitol can cause gas, diarrhea and IBS-like symptoms, and some people react at lower doses; a 1985 EU Scientific Committee on Food report said 50 g per day can cause diarrhea.[2] Xylitol is toxic to dogs, with insulin release and hypoglycemia reported at around 100 mg/kg and liver failure likely above 500 mg/kg; ferrets are also affected, while rhesus macaques, horses and rats are considered safe.[2] The US FDA considers xylitol safe as a sugar substitute.[2]

Sugar-free gum became a mainstream product category, and xylitol is the sweetener in several dental-positioned brands. On T Nation forums, members have recommended xylitol gum as a snack that supports teeth, with one writing that xylitol has been shown to reduce decay-associated bacteria, and others noting that it is used in common sugarless gum and is said to lower ear-infection risk in children.[14][15]

A maternal randomized trial of 107 pregnant women with high salivary mutans streptococci compared xylitol gum with no gum from the sixth month of pregnancy and reported lower transmission of the bacteria to children, which is part of why xylitol gum features in public-health caries discussions.[13]

Human trials include the 132-person dose-response study of mutans streptococci,[1] a randomized study in 80 young adults comparing xylitol and probiotic gums,[3] a 24-month school-based caries trial,[4] a 1984 trial on plaque and saliva S. mutans,[5] and a 857-child trial of xylitol products for otitis media.[6] Reviews of sugar substitutes and chewing gum for caries have also been published.[7] Wikipedia notes that evidence for xylitol products other than fluoride toothpaste is considered insufficient by the Cochrane review.[2]

lore.intro: On fitness and appearance forums xylitol gum appears as a cheap add-on for teeth and a replacement for sugary snacks.[14][15]

claims.believers: Forum members say xylitol has been shown to reduce decay bacteria and recommend chewing it daily.[14]
claims.experts: Systematic reviews report lower mutans streptococci in most xylitol trials versus sorbitol gum.[9]

claims.believers: Users cite brand claims that xylitol has cavity-fighting properties.[15]
claims.experts: A 2020 meta-analysis found tentative evidence of a caries reduction with high heterogeneity, and the 2015 Cochrane review cited by Wikipedia considered evidence for most xylitol products insufficient.[11][2]

claims.claim: Xylitol gum helps with ear infections in children
claims.believers: Forum posts note that xylitol is said to decrease ear infection risk.[15]
claims.experts: A 1998 randomized day-care trial tested xylitol for acute otitis media; Wikipedia reports that in 2011 the European Food Safety Authority rejected a health claim that xylitol gum prevents middle-ear infections.[6][2]
